nodes.focus: Character, duties, and competence of the people or organizations who develop, deploy, or oversee AI.

nodes.label: Action
nodes.focus: Rightness of the act itself, independent of realized harm (deontological).

nodes.label: Outcome
nodes.focus: Foreseeable or actual impacts and harms (consequentialist).

nodes.label: Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
nodes.moral_rationale: The duty is not to perform the listed acts. Claimed benefits do not reopen the ban. Actor duties (who must refrain) and outcome concerns (why these acts were listed) are secondary to the prohibition itself.

nodes.label: Article 6: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
nodes.moral_rationale: Risk class follows foreseeable harm potential of the use case or product role, not the character of the provider or a blanket ban on a technique.

nodes.label: Article 9: Risk management system
nodes.moral_rationale: The organizing logic is residual risk to health, safety, and fundamental rights. Mandatory process steps are the means; named provider duties are the carrier of those means.

nodes.label: Article 10: Data and data governance
nodes.moral_rationale: Provider data-governance duties (actor) and mandated examination practices (action) both serve bias and performance outcomes. No single dimension dominates.

nodes.label: Article 14: Human oversight
nodes.moral_rationale: The core duty is to build and operate a human-oversight gate. Competence of the overseer matters, but the requirement is structured as a mandatory process and design rule.

nodes.label: Article 15: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
nodes.moral_rationale: Performance and resilience thresholds against foreseeable failure and attack modes are the organizing logic. Process and provider duties exist to produce those outcomes.

nodes.label: Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
nodes.moral_rationale: The article assigns a bundle of duties to the deployer role. Process and monitoring requirements are substantial, but the defining move is naming who is obligated.

nodes.label: Article 53: Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models
nodes.moral_rationale: Duties attach to the GPAI provider role (documentation, transparency, cooperation). Systemic-risk overlays add outcome pressure, but the article is structured as provider obligations.

nodes.label: Article 72: Post-market monitoring by providers
nodes.moral_rationale: Continuous observation of real-world performance and emerging harms is the point. Provider and process duties exist to make that observation happen.

nodes.label: Principle 1.4: Robustness, security and safety
nodes.moral_rationale: The principle is framed around foreseeable adverse conditions and unreasonable safety risk. Override, repair, and decommission are mandated capabilities in service of that outcome. Cross-cutting soft law that most national robustness rules reuse.

nodes.label: Principle 1.5: Accountability
nodes.moral_rationale: Accountability attaches to AI actors according to role and context. The principle names who must answer, not which acts are banned or which harm thresholds apply.

nodes.label: GOVERN 1.1: Legal and regulatory requirements incorporated into AI risk policies
nodes.moral_rationale: Organizational duty to know and manage applicable AI law. The act of incorporating requirements into policy is mandated; harm outcomes are upstream of this control.

nodes.label: GOVERN 1.6: Roles and responsibilities for AI risk management
nodes.moral_rationale: The requirement is to name accountable roles. Process documentation is the vehicle; outcome thresholds are not the subject.

nodes.label: MAP 1.5: AI system impacts on individuals, groups, and society
nodes.moral_rationale: Impact characterization is consequentialist by design: the requirement exists to surface foreseeable harms and benefits.

nodes.label: MEASURE 2.6: AI system privacy risk measurement
nodes.moral_rationale: Measurement is keyed to privacy-related impacts. Mandated assessment practice supports that outcome focus.

nodes.label: MANAGE 2.4: Risk treatment responses documented and monitored
nodes.moral_rationale: Residual risk acceptance and ongoing monitoring center foreseeable impacts. Named ownership and process steps carry the outcome duty.

nodes.label: Section III: Effective challenge
nodes.moral_rationale: Effective challenge is defined by who challenges (informed, objective parties with stature) and the critical-analysis practice they must perform. Harm outcomes motivate the duty but do not structure the section.

nodes.label: Section IV: Model development, implementation, and use
nodes.moral_rationale: The section mandates development and use practices. Outcome concerns (model purpose fitness) matter, but the text is organized as required process for building and deploying models.

nodes.label: Section V: Model validation and ongoing monitoring
nodes.moral_rationale: Performance monitoring and outcomes analysis are the organizing logic. Independence of validators is a material actor duty supporting that outcome focus.

nodes.label: Section VI: Governance, policies, and controls
nodes.moral_rationale: Board and senior-management accountability and role clarity define the section. Policies and controls are the mandated acts those actors must maintain.

nodes.label: Section VII: Vendor and other third-party models
nodes.moral_rationale: Responsibility stays with the institution regardless of who built the model. Due diligence and monitoring practices serve that accountability, with risk-commensurate intensity pointing at outcomes.

nodes.label: Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
nodes.moral_rationale: Accountability and controller duties name who must comply; the principles are mandatory processing acts. Harm to data subjects motivates the regime but the article is organized as required practice plus accountable actors.

nodes.label: Article 22: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
nodes.moral_rationale: The duty is structured as a prohibited or constrained act (solely automated significant decisions) plus contestability safeguards. Actor rights and significant effects are material but the organizing rule is the decision practice itself.

nodes.label: Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
nodes.moral_rationale: High-risk to rights and freedoms is the trigger. Mandatory assessment process and controller ownership carry that outcome focus.

nodes.label: 45 CFR 164.308: Administrative safeguards
nodes.moral_rationale: Named organizational duties and mandated safeguard practices dominate. Confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI are the protected outcomes those acts serve.

nodes.label: 45 CFR 164.312: Technical safeguards
nodes.moral_rationale: The section mandates specific technical control practices. Outcomes (protect ePHI) motivate the rule; named actors are secondary to the required safeguards.

nodes.label: Five principles: Cross-cutting principles for UK AI regulation
nodes.moral_rationale: Accountability and governance name who must act inside existing regulator remits. Safety and fairness point at outcomes; transparency and contestability are mandated process rights.

nodes.label: Regulator-led delivery: Sector regulators deliver AI duties
nodes.moral_rationale: The design choice is who enforces (existing sector regulators and accountable firms). Process adaptation inside remits is secondary; harm outcomes are left to sector context.

nodes.label: Training data and model duties: Lawful training data and security assessment
nodes.moral_rationale: Mandatory provider practices for data and assessment dominate. Provider identity matters; content and rights harms motivate the duties.

nodes.label: Content labeling: Synthetic content labeling and safety
nodes.moral_rationale: Labeling and content-safety bans are mandated acts aimed at preventing harmful outputs. Provider role is the carrier, not the moral center.

nodes.label: Algorithmic Impact Assessment: Algorithmic Impact Assessment requirement
nodes.moral_rationale: Impact level and foreseeable effects on clients organize the duty. Named institutional owners and mandatory AIA process support that outcome focus.

nodes.label: Notice and explanations: Transparency and explanation to affected persons
nodes.moral_rationale: Notice and explanation are mandated communicative acts. Institutional accountability and client impact are material supports.

nodes.label: Access Control domain: Access control for CUI environments
nodes.moral_rationale: Required access-control practices are the organizing logic. Named contractor accountability and CUI confidentiality outcomes support those acts.

nodes.label: Audit and Accountability domain: Audit logging and accountability
nodes.moral_rationale: Traceability to accountable parties is the moral center. Mandatory logging practices implement that actor duty; mission harm is upstream context.

nodes.label: Investor-interest conflicts: Firm vs investor conflicts in PDA/AI tools
nodes.moral_rationale: The proposed duty targets harmful conflict outcomes for investors and mandates elimination or neutralization practices. Firm accountability is the carrier.

nodes.label: National AI governance: National AI governance structure
nodes.moral_rationale: Named national and organizational accountability is the primary orientation. Process and risk duties follow from that structure.

nodes.label: Transparency and safety duties: Transparency and safety obligations
nodes.moral_rationale: Mandated transparency and safety practices aim at preventing significant rights and safety harms. Business accountability is material but secondary to the required acts and outcomes.

nodes.label: Accountability: Accountability principle
nodes.moral_rationale: Identifiable responsible parties define the principle. Oversight practices and outcome ownership are supporting duties.

nodes.label: Contestability: Contestability principle
nodes.moral_rationale: The principle mandates contestation processes for significant AI effects. Affected persons and harm stakes matter; the organizing requirement is the challenge practice.
